newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels suspend hostage talks to buy time.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels suspend hostage talks to buy time.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages suspended negotiations on Thursday to gain time to study the Peruvian government's latest proposals and not because they feared an attack, analysts said.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa said the rebels would not attend Friday's scheduled talks because the government planned to storm the Japanese ambassador's residence while they were absent.

But analysts were sceptical of Cerpa's claims that security forces had dug tunnels in order to enter the diplomatic mansion while he and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas met government officials at a safehouse across the street.

"I do not think the government would engage in such a flagrant contradiction ... appearing to be seeking a peaceful end while it dug tunnels for a completely military solution," political analyst Enrique Bernales told a local radio station.

At the last round of talks on Wednesday the government presented the MRTA with what President Alberto Fujimori called an "all-inclusive" proposal for a peaceful end to the siege. Cuba's President Fidel Castro on Monday accepted Fujimori's request to grant asylum to the 20-odd guerrillas holding the hostages if the two sides reach an accord.

"Most likely the guerrillas are buying time to think about how they want to react to what's on the table," David Scott-Palmer, an author on Peru's guerrilla conflicts, said in a telephone conversation from Boston.

Despite the suspension of talks, he was optimistic. "We aren't hopelessly deadlocked. There had been some movement," he said. "While it does not sound hopeful we have learned that we cannot rely on public statements."
Some analysts think Cerpa is making up excuses to slow the talks and prolong his group's time in the media spotlight.

"(Cerpa) is having visions. He is trying to take advantage of the situation to grab the world's attention because he is at the centre of the news," former anti-terrorist police chief John Caro told local radio station RPP.

Caro said the government would not use tunnels in any case because an attack by air and over the perimeter walls would be easier. But security force sources confirmed the existence of at least four tunnels that were dug while music was blasted from loudspeakers outside the besieged residence.
The tunnels would be used in the case of an eventual attack that experts say would last about seven minutes but would result in a high death toll, the sources added.
The surprise suspension of talks dashed hopes ragiven no ground on the main demand of the guerrillas -- the release of jailed MRTA comrades.
Some Peruvians say it is time to concede on this issue.

"Seeing that almost three months have passed, we must unfortunately recognise that concessions have to be made," said Ernesto de la Jara, director of the Legal Defence Institute, a human rights organisation.
